fields.title: Who You Are and What You Are Allowed
fields.keyTakeaway: Authentication answers the question "who", authorization answers "what is allowed", and these are different screens with different user actions.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: What is the difference between "failed to sign in" and "access denied"?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Mixing these two concepts creates interfaces that lead the user in circles: a person with insufficient rights is prompted to sign in again, signs in, and gets rejected again. This was covered from the code side in `IN1-N3-L1`, and here it is covered from the mechanics side.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: **[[authentication|Authentication]]** is establishing who is in front of us. Signing in with a password, an SMS code, or biometrics.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **[[authorization|Authorization]]** is determining what this subject is allowed to do. It happens after authentication and during every operation.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: Different questions, different answers, different screens.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: *Knowledge.* Password, PIN. *Possession.* Phone, key, authenticator app. *Inherence.* Fingerprint, face.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: **[[2fa-mfa|Two-factor authentication]]** uses two factors from different categories. Password plus SMS code is knowledge plus possession. Password plus security question is two instances of knowledge, meaning it is not two-factor.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: A **[[session|session]]** is the state of presence after signing in. It is usually implemented as a pair: a short-lived [[access-token|access token]] and a long-lived [[refresh-token|refresh token]]. The short lifespan of the first limits damage in case of theft; the second avoids forcing the person to sign in every hour.
fields.sections/2/blocks/8/text: *Lifespan.* A compromise between security and convenience. Bank app means minutes, social network means months. *What happens on device change.* Keep sessions active or terminate them. *[[revocation|Access revocation]].* The ability to terminate a session: upon password change, sign out, or suspicion. A list of active sessions with a "terminate" button is a product feature that builds trust.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Signing in by phone number with a code is a single factor of possession. For buyers, this is enough: the cost of compromise is limited to order history and a saved card, which is protected by confirmation itself.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: The partner account requires a password plus a code; two-factor is mandatory. The stakes are different here: access to revenue, data exports, and settings.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: The access token lives for 15 minutes, the refresh token for 60 days. When the password is changed, all refresh tokens are revoked.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: The active sessions screen was added after a request from partners: a chain wanted to see which employees had signed in. It also turned out to be useful for buyers — 3% use it, and these are the ones who care about security.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: Distinguishing `401` and `403` in the interface: an expired session leads to sign-in while preserving what the person was doing; insufficient rights show an explanation and do not prompt to sign in.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Two-factor authentication increases security and decreases sign-in conversion. Deciding where it is mandatory and where it is optional is a product decision.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Authentication answers the question "who", authorization answers "what is allowed", and these are different screens with different user actions.
